# How to Design a Website Yourself: A 2026 Step-by-Step Guide

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/designing-a-website/
Published: July 6, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: Web Design

I run a web design studio in Kolkata. This post explains how to build a website without me.

That sounds like a bad business decision, so let me explain it. A large share of the people who ask about a website do not need an agency yet. They need one page, a domain, a working contact form, and something to send people to. Charging design fees for that is how studios get a reputation for selling things nobody asked for, and it is why I would rather tell you plainly where the line sits.

So here is the honest version of the DIY guide. Which builders are worth your money in 2026, what they actually cost on the day I checked, which one is quietly dying, and the specific point where doing it yourself stops saving money and starts costing you customers.

## The short answer

If your website is a business card, build it yourself. A one-page or five-page site with your services, your proof, and a way to contact you is well within reach of a beginner on Wix, Squarespace, WordPress.com or Carrd, and you will get it live in a weekend. If your website is a sales channel, meaning revenue depends on it ranking, converting, or looking different from your competitor, DIY becomes the expensive option, because you end up paying for a redesign later on top of everything you already paid.

The dividing line is not budget. It is whether the site has a job that can fail.

The rest of this guide is the how, with prices I read on each company's own pricing page on 30 July 2026.

## Where DIY is genuinely the right call

I will argue against my own invoice here, because pretending builders are toys is how agencies lose trust.

- You are testing whether the business works at all. Spending on custom design before you have a single paying customer is putting the roof on before the walls.

- The site is a formality. A local service business that needs an address, hours, a phone number and a form. A builder does this perfectly well.

- You are the product. Freelancers, consultants, photographers, coaches. A clean template with your work in it beats an expensive site with nothing in it.

- You genuinely enjoy it. Some founders like building their own site and keep it updated because of that. An agency site they cannot edit goes stale in four months.

If any of those describe you, stop reading comparison posts and go build the thing. Seriously. You do not need us.

## Where DIY stops being the right call

The reverse is just as specific, and this is the part most DIY guides will not tell you because they earn a commission on the builder signup.

- You look identical to your competitor. Every builder generates from the same patterns. Same hero, same three columns, same rounded cards. For a prototype nobody cares. For a brand, that is the entire problem. I have written about this in more detail in AI website builders versus custom development.

- The site has to sell something complicated. If a visitor needs to understand a service before buying it, the writing and the sequence of the page matter more than the template. That is strategy work, and no drag-and-drop editor does it for you.

- Search and AI visibility are the point. If you need Google and AI assistants to find and quote you, structure, speed and crawlability stop being cosmetic.

- You have outgrown the plan. The moment you are paying for the top tier of a builder plus three paid apps to work around its limits, you are paying agency money for template output.

The template versus custom decision has its own trade-offs, and I have laid them out honestly in template versus custom web design. Either answer can be correct. Choosing without knowing which one you picked is the mistake.

## What a website builder costs in 2026

Every price below was read on the company's own pricing page on 30 July 2026. Builder pricing moves faster than any blog post, so treat this as a snapshot and check before you pay.

One thing worth knowing before you compare: some of these companies show Indian pricing and some do not. Squarespace, WordPress.com and Framer served rupee prices. Wix, Webflow, Weebly and Carrd showed dollars. Wix states on its pricing page that prices and currency vary by location, that the dollar figures are shown for reference only, and that the final price appears on the purchase page before payment. You will not know what Wix costs you in rupees until you are at checkout.

Read that last row again. Carrd's Pro Standard plan, which includes a custom domain, forms and analytics, is $19 for a whole year. Wix Light is $17 a month, which is $204 a year. That is more than ten times the price for a one-page site. If all you need is one page, the cheapest correct answer is embarrassingly cheap.

### Wix

If you read an older guide that told you to buy the Wix Combo plan, throw that guide away. There is no plan called Combo on Wix's pricing page today. The lineup is Free, Light at $17 a month, Core at $29, Business at $39 and Business Elite at $159, with an Enterprise tier on request. Those are yearly-subscription prices paid in full up front, before tax. WebsiteBuilderExpert's Wix pricing guide, updated 3 February 2026, lists the same four plans at the same four prices, which is a useful second reading.

Wix now advertises over 2,000 templates and an AI builder that generates a site from a single prompt, then hands you the drag-and-drop editor to fix what it got wrong. That second half matters more than the first. The generated site is a starting point, not a finished one.

Wix is the most capable of the mainstream builders and the one I would pick if I had to bet on longevity. It reported $541.2 million of revenue in the first quarter of 2026 and $1.903 billion of annual recurring revenue, both up double digits year on year. It is not going anywhere.

What it is not: cheap at the top, or portable. Business Elite works out to $1,908 a year, and there is no meaningful way to take your design somewhere else when you leave.

### Squarespace

Squarespace still has the best templates of the mainstream builders, and that has been true for a decade. The Indian pricing page shows three tiers billed annually: Basic at Rs 630 a month, Core at Rs 720, Advanced at Rs 1,100. Every site starts with a 14-day free trial and no card required. There is no permanent free plan.

The detail that catches people out is the transaction fee. Basic charges 2% on online store sales. Core and Advanced charge 0%. If you sell anything at all, Basic is the expensive plan.

Two things worth knowing about the company. It was taken private by Permira in October 2024 in a deal worth about $7.2 billion and is no longer listed on the New York Stock Exchange, which is why nobody can quote you a current subscriber number. And in July 2026 it raised prices on its US annual plans by up to 26%, according to PetaPixel's report of 17 July 2026, with Core going from $23 to $29 a month. Squarespace did not publish a memo about it. Customers found out by email.

That is the builder subscription model showing its teeth. Your rent went up and you were told after the decision was made.

### Weebly

Do not start a new website on Weebly in 2026. I know older versions of this guide recommended it as the budget pick. That recommendation has expired.

Weebly is still on sale. The pricing page lists Free, Personal at $13 a month billed annually, Professional at $15 and Performance at $32, and the footer still reads Square, Inc. Signup still works, though it now routes you through creating a Square account rather than a Weebly one, which tells you where the product sits inside the company.

What has changed is that Square is not building it any more. SiteBuilderReport's review, updated 7 January 2026, documents the state of it: no new feature in over a year, no new theme in years, the Weebly community forum folded into Square's forum, and dormant social accounts. On Square's own community forum, a Square staff member responded to shutdown rumours in April 2025 with a line that is more revealing than reassuring: "Weebly is NOT suddenly closing or shutting down. Square is managing a gradual migration process." Existing sites keep working. The direction of travel is Square Online.

A platform in gradual migration is a fine place to keep an old site running and a poor place to start a new one. You would be building on ground the owner has already decided to leave.

### WordPress.com, Framer, Webflow and Carrd

Four more worth knowing about, because the Wix-Squarespace-Weebly trio stopped being the whole market years ago.

WordPress.com starts at Rs 200 a month for the Personal plan billed annually, Rs 350 for Premium and Rs 800 for Business, before tax. The free plan exists but shows WordPress.com's own ads on your site. Its pitch now includes a guided AI builder that, in its own words, lets you skip the blank screen and launch a site by chatting with AI. Business unlocks plugins, which is the tier where it becomes a real CMS rather than a blog host. If you want to understand the platform trade-offs before committing, our comparison of CMS platforms covers them.

Framer is the designer's builder. Free to try with 500 credits, then Rs 361 a month for Basic and Rs 1,084 for Pro, billed yearly. Its AI features run on a credit system, so heavy use costs extra on top of the plan. Beautiful output, steeper learning curve than Wix.

Webflow is the closest thing to real code without writing it. Starter is free on a webflow.io domain, Basic is $15 a month billed yearly and Premium is $25. Then it jumps, hard: the next tier up is Team at $2,500 a month on an annual contract. Webflow is excellent, and it is not a beginner's first website.

Carrd is the one nobody mentions and half of you actually need. Free for up to three sites, $9 a year for Pro Lite, $19 a year for Pro Standard with a custom domain, forms and analytics, $49 a year for Pro Plus. One page, done properly, for the price of two coffees a year.

## What changed in 2026: the first ten minutes are now AI

If you last built a website three years ago, the opening of the process is unrecognisable. You no longer start with a template gallery. You start with a text box asking what your business does.

Wix generates a site from a single prompt. WordPress.com sells a guided builder as the way to skip the blank screen. Squarespace meters AI tools by credits across its plans. Framer runs agents on the same credit model.

This is genuinely useful and it is also where most DIY sites go wrong. The generator produces a complete-looking site in ninety seconds. It has a hero, an about section, three services and a testimonial slot. It looks finished. It is not finished. It is a filled-in template wearing your business name, and every competitor who typed a similar prompt got a similar site.

Treat the AI pass as the first draft that saves you an afternoon of layout work. The value you add is everything after it. Your actual photos instead of stock. Your actual prices. The objection your customers really raise, answered on the page where they raise it. That part has never been automated, and I do not think it is close.

## Before you open the editor: five questions

Skipping this is the single most common reason a DIY site has to be rebuilt. It takes twenty minutes.

### What is this website's job?

Not "to have a website". Pick one job. Get enquiries. Take bookings. Sell twelve products. Prove you are real to someone who already got your name from a friend. A site with one job can be judged. A site with no job cannot be improved, only redecorated.

### Who is arriving, and what do they already know?

Someone who searched your company name needs different things from someone who searched your service. The first needs proof, the second needs an explanation. If you only have the budget to write one page well, write it for whoever arrives most.

### What do your three closest competitors look like?

Open their sites. Note what every single one of them says, because that is the sentence you must not use. Note what none of them say, because that is your opening. This is fifteen minutes of work and it is the highest-return fifteen minutes in the whole project.

### How many pages does this genuinely need?

Most first websites need four: home, services, proof or portfolio, contact. Adding a blog you will not write and a team page with one person on it makes the site look smaller, not larger.

### Who updates it in six months?

If the answer is you, choose the builder with the editor you find easiest, not the one with the best reviews. An easy site that stays current beats a beautiful one that freezes. Our web design process guide goes deeper on the planning stages if you want the full version.

## How to design a website by yourself, step by step

### Step 1. Pick the builder that matches the job

Use the table above and pick on constraints, not on features. One page and a link in bio, Carrd. A portfolio or a shop with beautiful templates, Squarespace. Broadest capability and the largest app ecosystem, Wix. Wanting to own a real CMS and eventually move the content elsewhere, WordPress.com on the Business tier. Design-led and willing to learn, Framer.

Nearly every builder has a free tier or a trial. Build the same homepage twice on two of them before paying anyone. Two hours of that will teach you more than a week of comparison articles, including this one. If the whole idea of not writing code appeals, our no-code development guide maps the wider tool landscape.

### Step 2. Choose a domain name you will not regret

Short, sayable over the phone, and spelled the way it sounds. Keyword-stuffed domains stopped helping years ago and they make you sound like a directory listing. If you are the brand, use your name.

Buy it separately from your builder if you can. A domain registered at an independent registrar is yours and can be pointed anywhere. A domain locked inside a builder subscription is one more thing tying you to a platform you might want to leave. Most plans throw in a free domain for the first year and then charge renewal at their own rate, so check the renewal price, not the introductory one.

If your first choice is taken, change the word rather than adding a hyphen or a stray extension. Hyphens get lost every time someone says the address out loud.

### Step 3. Pick a template, then pick a shorter one

Choose a template by its structure, not its photos. Those photos are not yours and the site will look markedly worse the moment you swap in your own. Ask instead whether the layout has room for what you actually have. If you own four good photographs, a template built around twelve is a template that will always look half empty.

Pick the one closest to the content you already possess. Then delete a section. Almost every DIY site is one section too long.

### Step 4. Customise, but change only four things

Fonts, colours, spacing and photography. That is the entire kit for making a template look like it belongs to you, and it is where beginners overreach.

- Two fonts maximum. One for headings, one for everything else. The template's default pairing is usually fine.

- One accent colour. Use it for buttons and links and nothing else, so that clickable things are obvious.

- More space than feels right. Amateur sites are cramped. Increasing the gaps between sections is the cheapest quality upgrade there is.

- Real photographs. Your premises, your work, your face. A slightly imperfect real photo outperforms a flawless stock one, because visitors can tell the difference and quietly discount the stock.

Resist the urge to restyle every button. Consistency is what reads as professional.

### Step 5. Write the content before you fall in love with the layout

This is where most DIY projects stall, and it is worth naming why. Design is fun and writing is not, so people spend three evenings on a colour scheme and then paste in placeholder text that stays there for a year.

Write these first, in a plain document:

- One sentence saying what you do and for whom, with no adjectives in it.

- The three things a customer asks before they buy, answered plainly.

- Your proof. Client names, sample work, review counts, years in business. Whichever you honestly have.

- What you want the visitor to do next, phrased as an action.

Keep paragraphs short, use real subheadings so a scanner can find their answer, and cut every sentence that would be true of your competitor as well. Sentences that are true of everyone persuade nobody, and increasingly they do not get quoted by AI assistants either.

### Step 6. Add only the features you will use

Every builder has an app store, and every app store is designed to make you spend more. Four are usually enough at the start.

- A contact form that emails you somewhere you actually check.

- Analytics, so you know whether anyone is arriving and where they leave.

- Payments, only if you sell something today.

- Bookings, only if you take appointments.

Live chat, pop-ups, loyalty widgets and review carousels can wait until you have traffic to justify them. Each one slows the page and adds a monthly fee.

### Step 7. Check it on a phone, on a real phone

Modern builders output responsive layouts by default, so this step is no longer about writing media queries. It is about catching what the automatic layout got wrong: headlines that wrap into four lines, buttons too small to tap, tables that overflow, images cropped through someone's face.

Preview mode lies slightly. Publish, then open the site on your own phone on mobile data rather than office wifi, and try to complete the one action the site exists for. If you cannot do it in under a minute with your thumb, neither can your customer. Our guide to responsive web design covers what to look for in more detail.

### Step 8. Test the boring things

Click every link. Submit the form and confirm the email arrives, including in spam. Check the phone number is tappable. Read the page aloud once, because you will hear the awkward sentences you cannot see. Ask one person who is not you to find your price without guidance and watch where they hesitate.

Before you publish, set the page titles and descriptions. Builders default to something like "Home" and "Untitled", and that is the text that shows up in search results and when someone shares your link.

### Step 9. Publish, then plan the first edit

Publish is a button. The part people skip is what comes after. Put a recurring reminder in your calendar for a month from now to fix the one thing you already know is weak. Websites do not fail on launch day. They fail by being abandoned four weeks later.

## The part where I argue against myself

I said at the top that most small enquiries do not need an agency. That is true, and here is the other half of it.

The thing a studio sells is not the pixels. It is the decisions before the pixels. What are you selling, who is the competitor, who is the audience, what must this page communicate, where does that communication happen. A builder answers none of those questions. It executes an answer you supply. When the answer is thin, the site is thin, and it renders beautifully.

So the honest test is this. If you can answer the five questions in this guide clearly, build it yourself and put the money into photography and advertising instead. If you cannot answer them, no amount of subscription buys you the answer, and that is the moment a designer earns their fee. If you want to see what that costs before you enquire, we have published price ranges in our breakdown of web design costs in Kolkata, and the questions worth asking any studio are in questions to ask before hiring a web design agency.

One more thing, from experience I would rather not have. I lost two companies before Pixel Street, and the lesson that survived both is that you should never build your main asset on ground someone else controls. Every builder on this page is rented land. Squarespace raising prices by email in July 2026 and Square quietly parking Weebly are the same story told twice. Rent it while you are proving the idea. Own it once the idea is proven.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I really design a website by myself with no experience?

Yes, for a small site. A four-page business site on Wix, Squarespace or WordPress.com is achievable in a weekend by someone who has never done it before, and AI onboarding has cut the hardest part, the blank screen, down to a few minutes. What experience buys is not the building. It is knowing what to leave out. If you want to learn the craft properly rather than just ship one site, we keep a list of the best places to learn web design.

### What is the cheapest way to get a real website online?

On the prices I checked on 30 July 2026, Carrd Pro Standard at $19 a year is the cheapest route to a one-page site with a custom domain, forms and analytics. For a multi-page site, WordPress.com Personal at Rs 200 a month billed annually was the lowest rupee price of the builders I checked. Free plans work for practice, but they put someone else's branding or advertising on your site.

### Is the Wix Combo plan still available?

No. There is no plan called Combo on Wix's pricing page as of 30 July 2026. The current lineup is Free, Light at $17 a month, Core at $29, Business at $39 and Business Elite at $159, all billed yearly and paid up front. Any guide still quoting Combo pricing is at least a full plan generation out of date, which is a decent test of whether a comparison article has been checked recently.

### Should I still use Weebly?

Not for a new site. It is still sold and existing sites still work, but Square has it in gradual migration towards Square Online, and independent reviews in January 2026 found no new features for over a year and no new themes for years. If you already run a Weebly site that works, there is no emergency. If you are starting today, start somewhere with a future.

### How long does it take to build your own website?

The building is the short part. Expect a weekend for a small site if your content is ready, and several weeks if it is not, because writing the words and gathering photographs is what actually takes the time. That is the honest sequence: content first, then design, then launch.

### When should I stop and hire someone?

When the website has a job that can fail. If lost enquiries cost you more per month than a designer would, or if you are stacking paid apps onto a top-tier plan to work around limitations, DIY has stopped being the cheap option. That is the point to talk to a web design company rather than buy another add-on.

# Best Sites for Learning Web Design, Checked in 2026

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/best-sites-for-learning-web-design/
Published: July 6, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: Web Design

I run Pixel Street, a web design studio in Salt Lake, Kolkata. We design and build for Coca-Cola, ITC and Marico. Selling you on the idea that web design is too hard to learn yourself would be good for my business. I am going to argue the opposite, because the only thing that makes a list like this worth reading is whether the links still work.

A learning list with rotten links is worse for a beginner than no list at all, because a beginner cannot tell the difference between a dead resource and their own failure to understand it. Roundups do not get re-checked, and the links quietly go: a company folds, a channel changes subject, a domain gets parked.

So I opened every outbound link on this page on 30 July 2026, checked what each platform is now, and rebuilt the list around what survived. Every price below was printed on that company's own pricing page on that date. Where a company would not show me a price without an account, I have said so rather than guess. Rupee figures are what those sites quote to a visitor in India; dollar figures are what they quote in dollars.

## The short answer

If you are starting from zero with no budget, you do not need to spend anything at all. Work through freeCodeCamp's Responsive Web Design certification, use The Odin Project for the order to learn things in, and keep MDN open as your reference. That combination is a complete front-end education and all three are free.

Paid platforms earn their money for one reason: a gap you have already identified and can name. "I cannot get my head around CSS layout" is a gap. "I want to learn web design" is not, and a subscription will not fix it. Pay after you have hit a wall, not before.

One thing to settle before you start: decide whether you want to design websites or build them. They are related jobs with different day-to-day work, and we have written up the difference in web design versus web development. Most of the resources below teach both, badly labelled.

## What has died, moved or changed hands

This is the part no other roundup will tell you, so it goes first.

- Lynda.com no longer exists as a brand. Going to lynda.com now returns a 301 redirect to linkedin.com/learning. The library survived the move; the name did not. Watch out for lynda.com.cach3.com, which was never Lynda at all: it is a third-party static archive of the site as it looked in May 2019, and the page says so at the top.

- Udemy is now owned by Coursera. Coursera announced the all-stock combination on 17 December 2025 and closed it on 11 May 2026, at an implied equity value of roughly $2.5 billion. Udemy is a wholly owned subsidiary of Coursera, and the companies have said the two platforms will keep running separately while they work on a unified product.

- WebDesign.com is a parked domain. It is still recommended in places as a YouTube channel to follow. The domain now resolves to a holding page owned by Digimedia.com, L.P. carrying a one-line definition of the phrase "web design".

- TheNewBoston has moved on. Bucky Roberts' channel is still uploading, which is why a link checker would call it healthy. The three most recent uploads when I checked were episodes one, two and three of a bonsai gardening series from March 2026. It is not a programming channel any more.

- 1stWebDesigner's channel is effectively dormant. One upload in June 2025, and before that nothing since September 2020.

- Codecademy belongs to Skillsoft. The acquisition completed on 4 April 2022 and the footer of the site now reads "Codecademy from Skillsoft". The product is still good; the pricing has moved a long way in the years since people started recommending it.

- Flux Academy sells something completely different now. The 10k Website Process and The 6-Figure Freelance Designer are no longer sold under those names, and the $130 course tier is gone.

- Frontend Masters renamed itself Master.dev on 15 June 2026, on the grounds that "frontend" no longer described a catalogue that includes Go, Rust, cloud and AI. Old frontendmasters.com links still redirect, for now.

## Free, and better than most of the paid courses

### freeCodeCamp

Source: freecodecamp

freeCodeCamp now runs eleven certifications, all free, and each is built around roughly 300 hours of work and five projects you have to make pass a test suite. Start with Responsive Web Design. It covers semantic HTML, forms, accessibility, Flexbox and CSS Grid, which is the actual foundation of the job rather than a tour of it.

The reason I put this first is not the price. It is that the certification projects force you to produce finished work instead of watching someone else produce it. If you want to understand why the responsive part matters so much, we have a longer piece on responsive web design and what it involves in practice.

After Responsive Web Design, the natural next steps in their catalogue are JavaScript Algorithms and Data Structures, then Front End Development Libraries.

### The Odin Project

The Odin Project is a free, open-source curriculum that solves the problem freeCodeCamp does not: what to learn next, and in what order. It curates the best tutorials, articles and documentation that already exist and strings them into two paths, Full Stack JavaScript and Full Stack Ruby on Rails, with portfolio projects between the sections.

If you have ever opened twenty browser tabs, read four contradictory opinions on how to start, and closed all of them, this is the fix. Take the Full Stack JavaScript path unless you have a specific reason to want Rails.

### MDN Web Docs

MDN's Learn web development section is free, maintained by Mozilla and the MDN community, and is the closest thing the web has to an official manual. The core modules run from structuring content with HTML through CSS styling, CSS layout, dynamic scripting with JavaScript, accessibility, design for developers and version control.

Treat MDN as your reference rather than your course. When a tutorial tells you to write something and you want to know what that thing actually does, MDN is where you find out. It is the one link in this post I expect to still be correct in a decade.

### W3Schools

W3Schools has been running since 1999 and covers 60-odd languages with free tutorials and a try-it-yourself editor. It is unbeatable for answering one narrow syntax question in fifteen seconds, and it is a poor primary curriculum because it teaches you what is possible without teaching you what is wise. The site also now sells a W3Schools Plus subscription and paid certificates; I did not quote a price because I could not read one on their page.

### YouTube

Source: YouTube

YouTube recommendations rot faster than anything else on a list like this, as the dormant and repurposed channels above show. The one I would still point a beginner at is Flux Academy, which posted on the day I checked and posts most weeks. Ran Segall's videos are strongest on design judgement and the commercial side of the work, which is exactly the part written tutorials tend to skip.

The W3Schools channel still exists but has not published since February 2025, so use the website instead.

My rule for YouTube generally: check the upload date before you follow a tutorial. A CSS video from 2019 will teach you workarounds for problems that no longer exist.

## Paid platforms, and what each one actually buys you

### Codecademy

Source: codecademy

Codecademy's strength is still the in-browser editor: you type, it checks, you move on. That loop is genuinely good for a first week when a local development setup would only get in the way.

The free tier is thinner than its reputation. Codecademy's free plan is widely described as giving you access to most of the content. It does not. Basic gives you basic access to free courses, community support and reference material. Skill paths, career paths, real-world projects, assessments and certificates of completion all sit behind the paywall. Plus is Rs 300 a month billed annually, Pro is Rs 600 a month billed annually, and both roughly double if you pay monthly. Codecademy has been owned by Skillsoft since April 2022.

### Treehouse

Source: treehouse

Treehouse runs more than 60 tracks, and the ones relevant here are the 42-hour Web Design track, Front End Web Development, Design and Build a Website, and Web Programming Skills for Graphic Designers. That last one is the most interesting entry on their catalogue if you already design and want to stop handing files over a wall.

Pricing is Rs 1,650 a month for Courses and Rs 3,250 a month for Courses Plus, with a seven-day free trial. Their Techdegree bootcamp programmes are priced separately at $199 a month, which is a very different commitment and should be treated as one.

### Coursera, and Udemy

Source: coursera

Coursera works with more than 350 university and industry partners and puts over 10,000 courses behind Coursera Plus, which costs Rs 2,099 a month or Rs 13,999 a year. What you are buying is the name on the certificate. Google's and Meta's UX and front-end programmes live here, and that branding is worth something on a CV in a way that a platform-branded certificate usually is not.

Source: udemy

Udemy is now part of the same company. The merger closed on 11 May 2026 and Udemy operates as a wholly owned subsidiary of Coursera, with both platforms running separately for the moment. The model still differs: Udemy is a marketplace where you buy one course outright rather than subscribing, which suits a single narrow topic you want to own permanently.

I am not quoting Udemy prices. Their site blocks automated requests, so I could not read a current price from the page itself, and a price I cannot verify is not a price. Look at the course page before you buy, and note that the marketplace runs discounts constantly, so the number you first see is rarely the number you pay.

### LinkedIn Learning, formerly Lynda.com

Lynda.com as it was. Everything on that site now lives at LinkedIn Learning.

Lynda Weinman and Bruce Heavin's company was one of the originals in online video training, LinkedIn bought it, and the brand was folded into LinkedIn Learning. Typing lynda.com into a browser today just redirects you.

The platform now lists 25,900 courses and more than 1,300 curated learning paths, with a free first month. I have not put a subscription price in the table because LinkedIn will not show one without an account, and I am not going to print a figure I could not read.

What it is good at is breadth of software training, and the fact that a lot of employers already pay for it. Check whether you have access through work or a college before you pay for it yourself.

### Master.dev, formerly Frontend Masters

Frontend Masters became Master.dev on 15 June 2026. Same 300-plus courses, same instructors, broader catalogue that now runs past frontend into backend, cloud and AI. It costs $39 a month or $390 a year.

This is not a beginner platform and it is not trying to be. The courses are long, taught by working engineers, and assume you already write code. Buy a year of it when you have finished a free curriculum and want to go deep on one thing properly, not when you are still deciding whether you like this.

### Interaction Design Foundation

IxDF has been running since 2002 and now lists 41 courses and 159 master classes on UX, UI and product design. It also quietly moved house: interaction-design.org redirects to ixdf.org, so update any old bookmark.

Membership is Rs 650 a month for the Student plan or Rs 800 a month for Professional, both billed annually, with a 14-day money-back guarantee. At Indian pricing that is the cheapest structured UX theory on this list by a distance. The material is academic in tone, which is a strength if you want to understand why an interface works and a weakness if you want to be building by Friday.

### Flux Academy

Source: flux academy

Flux now sells membership rather than individual flagship courses. Foundation is $197 a quarter or $597 a year, Edge is $497 a quarter or $1,497 a year, and Accelerator is $1,667 a quarter or $4,997 a year, all with a 30-day money-back guarantee. The current catalogue covers the Webflow Masterclass, the Framer Masterclass, Figma For Web Designers, Web Design Masterclass, Brand Design Mastery, Core Design Skills, Freelancing for Web Designers, WriteSite and Web Strategy Master.

The honest framing: Flux teaches the commercial side of being a web designer, which is the part that decides whether you make a living. It is also priced in dollars, which makes it the most expensive thing on this list for anyone earning in rupees. Read the free YouTube material first and see whether the way he thinks matches how you want to work.

## Skills worth building, in order

Most skills lists for web designers are ten bullet points of nouns with no priority attached, which is useless to someone deciding what to open tonight. Here is the order I would defend.

- HTML and CSS, properly. Not enough to follow a tutorial. Enough to build a layout from a blank file and know why it holds together. Everything else is easier afterwards.

- Layout and typography. Spacing, hierarchy and type do more for how a site feels than colour or imagery ever will, and none of the platforms above teach this as well as looking hard at work you admire does.

- Figma. Learn one interface design tool well rather than three badly, and make it the one your collaborators already use. The fundamentals transfer; tools keep dying.

- Responsive behaviour and accessibility. These belong together because both come down to not assuming anything about the person on the other end.

- Enough JavaScript to be dangerous. You do not need to be an engineer. You need to know what is cheap to ask for and what is expensive.

- The process around the work. Briefing, scoping, review, handover. We wrote up how we run ours in our web design process guide.

If you want the thinking behind the craft rather than the mechanics, the reading list in our must-read books for web and graphic designers covers ground no video course does.

## Questions people actually ask

### Do I have to learn to code to be a web designer?

You have to be able to read it. A designer who cannot read HTML and CSS produces work that developers quietly redraw, and never finds out why the built site does not match the file. You do not need to be able to build a backend.

### Is a paid subscription worth it if I am earning in rupees?

Not at the start. The three free resources at the top of this list are not a compromise, they are the recommendation. The subscriptions worth considering on Indian pricing are Codecademy and IxDF, both of which quote in rupees and land under Rs 1,000 a month billed annually. Dollar-priced platforms are a different order of expense, and I would only reach for one after free material has stopped being enough.

### Which certificate gets you hired?

My honest opinion is that the certificate is not what convinces anyone. Finished work is. A certificate says you completed a course; three real projects with an explanation of the decisions behind them says you can do the job. If you are choosing between them anyway, a university or company-branded certificate on Coursera carries a name a stranger recognises, which a platform-branded one does not.

### How long does this take?

freeCodeCamp puts each of its certifications at about 300 hours. At ten hours a week, one certification is most of a year. Anyone selling you a career in six weeks is selling you something else.

### Why are some prices here in rupees and some in dollars?

Because that is what each company showed me. Codecademy, Treehouse, Coursera and IxDF quote Indian pricing to a visitor from India. Master.dev, Flux Academy and Treehouse's Techdegree quote in dollars. I have kept each one in the currency it was displayed in rather than converting, because exchange rates move and a converted number would be wrong by the time you read this.

## Where to go from here

Pick one of freeCodeCamp or The Odin Project tonight, keep MDN in a tab, and do not open a second course until you have finished the first. The failure mode for self-taught designers is not choosing the wrong platform. It is choosing four of them.

Every link on this page was checked on 30 July 2026. If you find one that has since gone stale, tell me and I will fix it, because that is the only thing that keeps a list like this honest.

If you would rather have the work done than learn to do it, our team at Pixel Street builds websites in Kolkata for brands you have heard of, and we are happy to talk.

## How to actually choose between them

The standard advice in this genre is to check experience, read reviews, get a free quote, compare prices, check the portfolio and ask for references. That is six items, it is really two, and one of the two is close to useless. Here is what I would actually do, having sat on the other side of this conversation for years.

### Ask to see the app in the store, not in a case study

A case study is a designed artefact. A store listing is not. Ask for the link, check who the developer of record is, read the recent one-star reviews, and look at the last update date. An app that has not shipped an update in two years tells you how that relationship ended.

### Ask who owns the code and the accounts

This separates a supplier from a landlord, and almost nobody asks it before signing. Whose Apple Developer account will your app live in? Whose Play Console? Who holds the repository, the signing keys, the push certificates? If the answer is the agency, you do not own your app. You are renting it, and the rent gets renegotiated the day you try to leave. I lost two companies before Pixel Street, and the lesson that survived both is that you never build your main asset on ground somebody else controls.

### Treat the free quote as the least informative thing you get

A quote produced before anybody has scoped your data model is a sales document, not an estimate, and comparing several of them mostly tells you who is most willing to guess low. For why the numbers in this city vary so wildly, see what web design costs in Kolkata. The same logic applies to apps.

### Decide first whether you need an agency at all

For a single well-defined app with a fixed scope, a good freelancer can be the better answer; for anything needing sustained maintenance an agency usually is. Freelancer versus agency covers that trade-off properly, and it is worth settling before you start taking meetings.

## Questions people actually ask

### Are these companies ranked?

No. They are listed alphabetically and I have deliberately made no quality judgement between them. I run a competing studio in the same city; any ranking I published would be worth exactly nothing to you, and every ranking you see elsewhere on this subject is built from the agencies' own marketing copy.

### Why is Pixel Street not on this list?

Because we do not build mobile apps. We do web design, branding and digital marketing. Adding ourselves to a list of app developers to catch the traffic would be the obvious move and also a lie.

### One of the sites here looks out of date. Should I rule the company out?

Not on its own. A stale copyright year means the marketing site is not anybody's priority, which is common at firms whose work all arrives by referral. It becomes a real signal when it stacks with others: an abandoned blog, no recent releases, a careers page frozen in time. Two companies here show that stacking, and I have said which.

### How often is this list checked?

Every company on it was fetched on 30 July 2026. Local agency lists rot faster than almost any other kind, so if you are reading this long after that date, open the sites yourself first. Four minutes, and it is the most useful thing you can do with this post.

### What if I need a website rather than an app?

Different job, different shortlist. We keep a separately verified list of SEO companies in Kolkata, and Pixel Street itself does web design and eCommerce work from Salt Lake.

## What this list is worth

Ten companies, ten sites opened on 30 July 2026, ten still trading. No rankings, no borrowed client logos, and no project counts I cannot stand behind. That gives you a verified starting point and nothing more, which is honestly all a list like this can be.

## How to choose one, from someone who pitches against these people

The standard advice is to pick an agency that understands your business, is creative, is strategic, is organised and is passionate about their work. Nobody has ever chosen an agency on that basis, because no agency has ever failed to claim all five. Here is what I would actually ask, and yes, I would be uncomfortable answering some of it.

### Ask who owns the ad accounts and the pages

This is the question that decides what happens when the relationship ends, and almost nobody asks it at the start. Whose Meta Business Manager holds your page? Whose ad account has your spend history and your pixel data in it? If the answer is the agency, then leaving means starting your audience data from zero, and every renewal conversation happens with that gun on the table. I lost two companies before Pixel Street, and the lesson that survived both was never to build your main asset on ground somebody else controls. A Business Manager you do not own is exactly that.

### Ask what they would refuse to do

An agency that will do anything you ask has no method. Ask what campaigns they have argued a client out of, and what they would tell you not to bother with. The useful answer is specific and slightly awkward. The useless answer is a list of services.

### Ask which metric they will be judged on before you sign

Follower growth is the metric agencies volunteer, because it is the one they can always deliver and the one least connected to revenue. Decide the number that actually matters to your business, whether that is qualified enquiries, cost per lead or repeat purchase rate, and get it into the agreement. If an agency resists that conversation, the resistance is your answer.

### Ask what happens when the platform changes

Reach on every major platform is set by algorithms nobody outside those companies controls, and they change without notice. The question is not whether an agency can promise results despite that. It is what they did the last time it happened. Anyone working in this field since 2023 has lived through a platform renaming itself and rebuilding its API access. Ask what that cost their clients and how they handled it.

### Then ask the general agency questions

Most of what separates a good agency engagement from a bad one is not specific to social media at all. We wrote those up in the questions worth asking before you hire an agency, and if search is also on your list, SEO companies in Kolkata is checked the same way this page is.

## Questions people actually ask

### Why is your own agency on this list?

Because we do the work, and leaving ourselves off a list of Kolkata social media agencies would be a different kind of dishonesty. What is missing is the advantage: no ranking, alphabetical order, our entry labelled as ours, and no client names or results claims on it, under the same rule that covers everyone else's.

### Is this list ranked?

No, and it should not be. I compete with these agencies. Any ranking I published would be worth nothing to you, and the rankings you find elsewhere on this subject are assembled from the agencies' own marketing copy or from whoever paid the directory.

### What happened to Digital Googly?

Its domain has nameservers but no address record, so nothing answers for it and the site cannot be loaded. I have no information about the company beyond that and have not guessed. If it returns, it can go back on.

### Two of these agencies have 2024 in the footer. Is that a problem?

Not by itself. Plenty of good agencies never touch their own site because all their work comes by referral. It is the cobbler's-children problem and it is real. It becomes a signal when it stacks with other things: an abandoned blog, no recent work, a careers page frozen in time. Neither of the two here shows that stacking.

### How current is this page?

Every agency on it was fetched on 30 July 2026. Local agency lists rot faster than almost any other kind of page, and one name here lost its website entirely. If you are reading this long after that date, open the sites yourself first.

## What this list is worth

Nine agencies, verified on one day, listed alphabetically, with the author's interest declared at the top rather than buried at the bottom. A tenth is absent because its website no longer exists. No borrowed client logo appears on it, ours included.

That is a less impressive page than a confident top ten. It is also the only version of it I would show to somebody I liked. If you want a social media marketing agency in this city, there are at least nine of us, and the one worth hiring is the one that answers the questions above without flinching.

# SEO vs Google Ads: Which One Should You Choose?

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/seo-vs-google-ads/
Published: July 6, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: Digital Marketing

I sell SEO retainers, so treat what follows with the suspicion it deserves. I am about to argue that the case for paying Google got stronger in 2026, and that the sentence my own industry has leaned on for fifteen years, that SEO is free traffic, is now doing more harm than good.

The standard version of this comparison describes SEO and Google Ads as two roughly equal doors into the same room, and settles the argument with a statistic about a Microsoft study claiming Google Ads take 63% of mobile clicks against 27% for organic. I went looking for that study and could not find it. What exists is two unrelated numbers from two unrelated sources, welded together somewhere in the content-mill supply chain and repeated ever since. I will not use it, and I am not replacing it with a friendlier guess.

The honest 2026 version of this comparison is less tidy, and it starts with what happened to the room.

## The short answer

Use Google Ads when you need demand you can switch on, measure and switch off. Build SEO when you want an asset that keeps working after the invoice stops. Most businesses with any budget at all end up running both.

What changed is the exchange rate. A top ranking used to convert into a fairly predictable number of visits. It does not any more, because Google increasingly answers the question on the results page and never sends the click. That does not make SEO worthless. It makes the case for SEO an argument about credibility and compounding rather than an argument about cheap clicks, and it means the paid side deserves a harder look than I used to give it.

## A first-place ranking buys fewer clicks than it used to

Two studies changed my mind on the detail here, and both published their method, which is the only reason I am willing to quote them.

The Pew Research Center tracked the real browsing behaviour of 900 US adults across 68,879 Google searches in March 2025. On searches that returned an AI summary, users clicked a traditional search result in 8% of visits. On searches without one, they clicked in 15%. Clicks on the links inside the AI summary itself: 1% (Pew Research Center, 22 July 2025).

The second finding is worse for the reassuring version of my sales pitch. Ahrefs looked at 863,000 keyword SERPs and found that 37.9% of the pages cited in AI Overviews also rank in Google's top 10, down from roughly 76% in July 2025 (Ahrefs, March 2026). Ranking and getting quoted have come apart. I have written about what that does to the whole discipline in AEO vs GEO vs SEO, and it is the single most useful companion piece to this one.

Put those two together and the organic side of this comparison now has a specific, measurable leak. Fewer clicks per ranking, and a ranking that no longer reliably buys you a place inside the AI answer either.

So when a proposal tells you SEO is free traffic, the correction is that SEO was never free. It was prepaid, in months of work, and the amount of traffic that prepayment buys per ranking has fallen. I still sell it. I sell it on different grounds now.

## Google Ads is not the product you last read about

Most comparison posts on this topic, including my own until today, describe a Google Ads that stopped existing years ago. If a proposal in front of you names a campaign type from the list below on the left, the person who wrote it has not opened the platform recently.

### Campaign types that were renamed or removed

What you may still hear it called
What Google calls it now

The pattern is not cosmetic. Every one of those changes moved a lever from the advertiser to Google's models. That is the real cost of Google Ads in 2026, and it does not appear on the invoice: you are buying outcomes with progressively less control over how they are produced.

### Ads now run inside the AI answer, and India is in the first cohort

This is the part that most directly changes the SEO versus Ads maths, and it is documented rather than rumoured.

Google's help centre states that ads are eligible to show above or below AI Overviews in all 200-plus markets where AI Overviews appear, and that ads run inside AI Overviews in English on mobile and desktop in twelve countries, India among them (Google Ads Help, About ads and AI Overviews). The eligible inventory is not a new product you have to buy: "Text and Shopping ads from existing Search, Shopping and Performance Max campaigns are eligible to show within the AI Overviews." Google says it withholds ads in sensitive verticals including finance, healthcare, gambling and politics.

For AI Mode, Google's own advertiser page describes formats still in testing, "powered by AI Max and Performance Max", and says they are "integrated directly into AI-generated responses" while labelled as ads (Google, Ads in AI Mode). I would not plan a budget around a format in testing. I would notice the direction.

Read that against the Pew number and the asymmetry is uncomfortable for my side of the business. The AI answer that is taking organic clicks is the same surface Google is filling with paid inventory, and an Indian advertiser is already inside that rollout rather than waiting for it.

## What clicks actually cost, and why I will not give you an India number

The only click-cost benchmark I am willing to put in this post comes with a published sample. WordStream analysed 13,474 US search advertising campaigns running from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 across 23 industries, reporting medians rather than means. Across all industries: cost per click $5.42, click-through rate 6.64%, conversion rate 8.18%, cost per lead $66.69 (WordStream, 19 May 2026).

Those are United States medians, useful for one thing only: seeing the shape of the spread between industries. Converting them to rupees produces a number that is wrong in a new and more confident way.

I went looking for an India equivalent while rewriting this. What I found were vendor pages quoting average Indian CPCs of ₹24, of ₹8 to ₹25, of ₹5 to ₹600, none naming a sample size, a date range or a method, several openly derived from US figures divided by an exchange rate. If an agency quotes you an "average India CPC" without saying where it came from, ask, because I could not find a source that survives the question.

The number you actually need takes twenty minutes. Open Keyword Planner, set the location to your city, enter the eight or ten keywords a customer would type before buying from you, and read the top-of-page bid range. That is your real starting CPC. Multiply by a conversion rate you are willing to defend, and you have a cost per lead you can compare against what a lead is worth. Every benchmark article on the internet is a worse input than that one exercise. If you want the same discipline applied to what the site itself should cost, I have broken that down in web design cost in Kolkata.

## SEO vs Google Ads, compared honestly

SEO

## Which one to start with

The generic advice, that new businesses should do SEO first because it is cheaper, is advice I used to give and now think is wrong more often than it is right. Here is how I would actually decide.

### Start with Google Ads if

- You need revenue inside the current quarter to keep the business alive. SEO cannot do that and pretending otherwise is a way to lose a client slowly.

- You do not yet know which of your services people actually search for. Two weeks of ad spend answers that question with real data, and the keyword list it produces is the honest input to an SEO plan.

- Your category is transactional and the buyer's search is unambiguous. Emergency plumbing, replacement parts, a specific product code.

- Your margin per sale comfortably exceeds a cost per lead you have calculated from Keyword Planner rather than from a blog post.

### Start with SEO if

- Your buyer researches for weeks before contacting anyone, which covers most B2B and most considered services. Nobody signs a branding retainer off a single ad click.

- You are being compared against three other firms and need to be the one that looks like it knows what it is talking about. That is a content problem, not a bidding problem.

- Your CPCs are genuinely punishing and your budget cannot absorb a learning period.

- You want to be quotable by AI assistants as well as rankable, which is now a separate job. My SEO checklist is the shortest honest starting point, and the advanced techniques list covers what comes after.

### Run both if you can

The strongest reason to run both is not synergy in the vague sense agency decks use it. It is that paid search tells you within weeks what organic search would have taken a year to teach you: which phrasings convert, which landing pages fail, which services people want that you have not written about. That feedback loop is worth money even when the ads themselves only break even.

## Three things you will hear about SEO that are not true

"SEO improves your Quality Score." It does not, at least not the way it is usually sold. Google lists three Quality Score components: expected click-through rate, ad relevance, and landing page experience (Google Ads Help). Your organic ranking is not among them. The overlap is real but narrower than the claim: a fast, relevant, genuinely useful landing page helps the third component, and SEO work tends to produce those pages. Ranking first for a keyword does nothing for the ad bidding on it.

"Organic traffic converts better than paid traffic." You will find this asserted confidently, and you will find the exact opposite asserted just as confidently, usually with nothing cited for either. Relative conversion rates depend on your offer, your intent mix and your landing pages, and any blanket figure you see quoted for this is describing somebody else's account.

"SEO keeps working for years after you stop." Half true, and less true every year. Rankings do decay slowly rather than instantly, and that is the real advantage. But a ranking you stop maintaining now depreciates on two axes rather than one, because the clicks each ranking earns are falling underneath it. Where search is heading covers that trajectory in more detail.

## What I would tell a founder over a coffee

Google Ads buys you attention. SEO buys you the right to be believed once you have it. In 2026 the first is easier to price and the second is harder to defend than it was, and I would rather say that out loud than keep selling the comfortable version.

The thing that has not changed at all is what both channels land on. Every click, paid or organic, arrives at a page. If that page is slow, unclear, or says the same thing as four competitors, no amount of bidding or ranking fixes it. Google's own generative-AI guidance, published in May 2026, makes the same point about AI search: creating content people find "unique, compelling, and useful" will influence your presence "more than any of the other suggestions in this guide" (Google Search Central). That is not an SEO tactic. It is the whole argument.

## FAQ

Is SEO still worth it in 2026?

Yes, on narrower grounds than the ones usually offered. It is no longer reliable as a cheap-clicks strategy: Pew found users click a traditional result on 8% of searches carrying an AI summary against 15% of those without, and Ahrefs found only 37.9% of AI Overview citations come from top-10 pages, down from about 76% in July 2025. What SEO still does better than paid search is build the credibility that makes people, and increasingly machines, choose you when they compare.

Which is cheaper, SEO or Google Ads?

Neither, reliably. SEO is a fixed monthly cost that does not scale with traffic won; Google Ads is a variable cost per click set by auction competition in your category. The comparison only becomes real once you have your own numbers: pull top-of-page bid ranges for your keywords in Keyword Planner, and compare the implied cost per lead against what a lead is actually worth to you.

Do Google Ads appear inside AI Overviews in India?

Yes. Google's help centre lists India among the countries where ads show within AI Overviews in English on mobile and desktop, and states that text and Shopping ads from existing Search, Shopping and Performance Max campaigns are eligible. Ads above and below AI Overviews are available in all 200-plus markets where AI Overviews run. Google says it does not show ads in AI Overviews for sensitive verticals such as finance, healthcare, gambling and politics.

Do Smart Shopping campaigns still exist?

No. Smart Shopping and Local campaigns were upgraded to Performance Max, with automatic upgrades completed by the end of September 2022. Standard Shopping campaigns do still exist and remain a legitimate choice when you want control over which products get spend. Discovery campaigns are gone too, folded into Demand Gen, and Dynamic Search Ads are being replaced by AI Max for Search campaigns.

Does SEO improve my Google Ads Quality Score?

Not directly. Quality Score is made of expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing page experience. Organic ranking is not an input. The genuine overlap is landing page quality, which good SEO work tends to produce anyway, so the benefit is real but much smaller than the claim usually implies.

If I can only afford one, which do I pick?

Pick Google Ads if you need revenue this quarter, if your buyer's search intent is unambiguous, and if your margin covers a cost per lead you have calculated yourself. Pick SEO if your buyer researches for weeks, if you are routinely compared against competitors before anyone makes contact, or if your category's CPCs are high enough that a learning period would eat the whole budget.

At Pixel Street we build the sites both channels land on, in Salt Lake, Kolkata, for clients including Coca-Cola, ITC and Marico. If you want a straight answer about which channel your business should start with, and are willing to hear it when the answer is not the one you were hoping for, get in touch.

# Shopify vs Adobe Commerce (Magento): Which Should You Build On?

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/shopify-vs-magento/
Published: July 6, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: E-COMMERCE

Most people who write to me about Magento are asking about a product that has not been sold under that name since April 2021.

I run Pixel Street, a web design studio in Salt Lake, Kolkata. We design and build for brands like Coca-Cola, ITC and Marico, so platform arguments land in my inbox most weeks. Almost every comparison of these two is written as a scorecard: thirteen rounds, a winner announced in each one, a champion crowned at the end. That format measures the wrong things, and it is how a wrong number survives for years without anybody checking it.

So start with the number. You will read in a great many places that Magento Commerce “starts at around $22,000/year for smaller businesses”. That figure cannot be traced to Adobe. Nobody can trace it, because Adobe does not publish a price at all. Further down I show exactly where it came from.

## The short answer

Shopify is a subscription with a published price. Adobe Commerce is a sales conversation with a quote attached to your revenue. Magento Open Source is free software that bills you in engineering time instead of licence fees, and Adobe now keeps it at arm’s length. For a small or mid-sized Indian brand without an in-house development team, Shopify is the honest default, and the real money leaks through payment fees rather than the plan price. If you have a large catalogue, complicated B2B pricing rules, or a team that already runs PHP infrastructure, ask Adobe for a quote and compare it against three years of your own developer time. Everything below is the detail behind that.

## The names changed, and the names decide what you are buying

Adobe acquired Magento in 2018. In April 2021 it folded the paid product into its own brand, and Magento Commerce became Adobe Commerce. The free edition kept the old name. Adobe still writes “Magento Open Source” in its current documentation, and still treats it as a separate code base from the paid product.

So “Shopify vs Magento” is really three products in a trench coat:

- Shopify. Hosted, subscription, priced in public.

- Adobe Commerce. The licensed enterprise product, sold as self-managed or cloud software, and since 2025 also as Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service. Adobe’s documentation for that SaaS edition, last updated 11 May 2026, describes a fully headless platform with continuous updates, a 30-day sandbox window before an update lands in production automatically, and a 99.9% availability commitment.

- Magento Open Source. Free to download, yours to host, patch and staff.

The rename is not trivia. It changed who the product is sold to. Adobe sells to enterprises with procurement departments, and the platform’s footprint reflects that. In the W3Techs survey dated 30 July 2026, Shopify was running 5.3% of all websites and Adobe Commerce 0.3%. Among sites where the content management system is known, that is 7.6% against 0.4%. W3Techs has even relabelled its entry from Magento to Adobe Commerce.

None of that makes Adobe Commerce a bad platform. It makes it a platform for a specific kind of company, and most of the businesses asking me the question are not that company.

## About that $22,000: what Adobe Commerce actually costs

Adobe does not publish a price for Adobe Commerce. There is no plan grid, no per-month tier to link to. The licence is quoted per customer and the quote is built around your gross merchandise value.

The $22,000 comes from agency blogs. The most linked of them is a Magento development agency’s pricing explainer, updated 8 July 2026, which prints a ladder: $22,000 a year under $1M GMV, $32,000 to $5M, $49,000 to $10M, $75,000 to $25M, $125,000 above that. Read the small print on that same page and it says the figures are “given purely for illustrative purposes and does not indicate the exact figures of the vendor”. It is one agency’s illustration of a budget conversation. It was never an Adobe price, and it travelled from blog to blog until it turned up in comparison articles wearing a tie.

I am not replacing it with a better guess. Here is the rule I use instead, and I would apply it to any enterprise software: if the vendor does not publish a price, the number is not the number. Get the quote, then add the parts the quote never covers. On the Adobe side that means hosting or cloud fees, the implementation build, extensions, and a retainer for upgrades, because a platform that ships versioned releases needs someone to install them.

The comparison people should be running is not licence against licence. It is three years of Shopify plus fees against three years of Adobe licence plus hosting plus a development team. That second column is where the real spend sits, and it is the column agencies like mine are usually being hired to fill. I would rather say that plainly than sell you a platform on a number nobody can source.

## What Shopify costs in India, including the part the pricing page does not add up for you

Shopify publishes its plans, which already puts it ahead on honesty. These are the figures on Shopify’s India pricing page as of 30 July 2026.

Plan

Billed yearly
