Plus
from ₹1,75,000/month
quoted per customer
0.2%

There is a three-day free trial and an introductory rate of ₹20 a month for the first three months, and Shopify POS Pro is ₹7,000 a month per location on top.

Now the part that matters here and gets skipped in most comparisons written for a US audience. That last column is the fee Shopify charges when you use a payment provider other than Shopify Payments. Shopify Payments is available in a fixed list of countries and regions, and India is not one of them. An Indian merchant is in that last column permanently.

Stack the arithmetic. On Basic, Shopify takes 2% of every order for using an outside gateway. Razorpay charges 2% on domestic cards, UPI and netbanking, plus 18% GST on that fee, and up to 3% on international cards. On a month of ₹10,00,000 in sales that is roughly ₹20,000 to Shopify, ₹20,000 to the gateway and ₹3,600 of GST on the gateway fee. About ₹43,600 in transaction costs against a plan fee of ₹1,499. The subscription was never the expensive part.

That single fact reorders the decision. Moving from Basic to Advanced costs about ₹21,000 more a month on annual billing and cuts the Shopify fee from 2% to 0.6%. At ₹10,00,000 of monthly sales that saves ₹14,000, so it is not worth it. At ₹25,00,000 it saves ₹35,000, so it is. Work out your own crossing point before you pick a plan, because Shopify will not do it for you on the pricing page.

Magento Open Source charges no platform fee on transactions at all. Your gateway still charges you, but nobody takes a second cut for the privilege of processing a sale. On high volume that is real money, and it is the strongest financial argument the open-source side has.

An older capture of Shopify’s pricing page, kept here for the record. The plan names and figures in the table above are what the same page shows today. Source: www.shopify.com

## What Magento Open Source is in 2026

The free edition is alive, and it is more current than its reputation suggests. Version 2.4.9 shipped on 12 May 2026 with official support for PHP 8.5 and Symfony 7.4 LTS. If you last looked at Magento during the 1.x death march, that is a different piece of software.

What has changed is the support position, and this is the part to read carefully before you commit a five-year store to it. Adobe’s published support dates run in three-year windows from each release:

- 2.4.6: regular support ends 11 August 2026, which is days away as I update this in July 2026.

- 2.4.7: ends 9 April 2027.

- 2.4.8: ends 11 April 2028.

- 2.4.9: ends around May 2029.

Adobe offers an extra year of support at no cost on 2.4.6 and 2.4.7, and then states the limit in its own release policy: “Extended support security patches are available to Adobe Commerce customers only. They are not available for the Magento Open Source code base.”

Read that sentence twice if you are running the free edition. The safety net is a paid feature. When your version falls out of the window, patching is your problem, and an unpatched store that takes card payments is not a cost saving. If you go this way, budget a retainer for upgrades and read our guide to vulnerability assessment and penetration testing before you launch, not after.

There is also a community answer to all this. Mage-OS is a community-owned distribution built on the Magento Open Source 2.4.9 code base, run by an association with an elected board and explicitly not affiliated with Adobe. Its 3.2.0 release on 14 July 2026 carried the current Magento security patch. If you want the open-source path with a maintenance community rather than a vendor, that is where the people went.

## Where each one actually wins

### Who is going to run the store on Monday morning

Shopify is built so a non-technical person can add products, run orders and change a homepage banner without opening a ticket. Magento assumes a developer is available. That is not a knock on Magento, it is its design intent, and it is the single question that decides most of these projects. If the answer to “who updates this on Monday morning” is “our marketing executive”, the decision is already made.

Source: www.shopify.com

### Design and front-end control

Shopify themes are quick and constrained. You get a good store fast, and past a point you are writing Liquid and working around the platform’s assumptions. Magento gives you the whole front end, and Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service goes further by being headless, which means the storefront is yours to build in whatever framework you like.

The honest version of this trade-off: freedom is only worth what you can afford to use. A studio that will spend real time on the front end can make either platform look distinctive. A brand that wants a theme installed by Friday should buy the constrained one and spend the saved budget on photography.

Source: www.cloudways.com

### Payments and checkout

Both platforms connect to the gateways an Indian store needs. The difference is the platform fee described above: Shopify takes its cut on top of the gateway unless you are in a Shopify Payments country, and Magento takes nothing. Checkout control follows the same pattern. Shopify’s checkout is Shopify’s, which is good for conversion and bad for anyone who needs an unusual flow. Magento’s checkout is code, so it can be anything you can pay a developer to build.

Source: www.magic42.co.uk

### SEO, and the honest state of that argument

Comparisons of these two traditionally hand SEO to Magento, because it allows deeper URL and template control. That is still true, and it matters much less than it used to. Both platforms produce crawlable, editable pages. What decides visibility now is whether your product and category pages say something a machine can attribute to you: real specifications, real answers, real inventory data, rather than the manufacturer’s description that forty other retailers also pasted in.

Shopify’s constraints cost you a few structural options. Magento’s freedom costs you a developer every time you want a template changed. Neither of those is why a store ranks. If you want the platform-agnostic version of that argument, we wrote it up in our comparison of the major CMS platforms.

Source: www.contentkingapp.com/

### Performance, and who is awake at 2am

Shopify runs the servers, ships the patches and answers the pager. Adobe Commerce as a Cloud Service does the same for paying customers, with automatic updates and a stated 99.9% availability. Self-hosted Magento performs exactly as well as the hosting and the team you put behind it, which in practice means it is fast when someone is being paid to keep it fast and slow when that person leaves.

This is the least glamorous line in the comparison and the one that has ended the most projects I have seen.

Source: cdn.shopify.com

### Apps, extensions and dropshipping

Both ecosystems are large enough that “does an app exist” is rarely the deciding question. Shopify’s apps install in a click and bill monthly, so a store running fifteen of them has a second subscription bill worth auditing. Magento extensions are code you install and then own the consequences of, including at upgrade time.

If you meet a comparison that recommends Oberlo for dropshipping, check its date. Shopify sunset Oberlo, and its staff announced in May 2022 that the last day of access would be 15 June 2022, with DSers as the migration partner. The dropshipping category on Shopify is now served by third-party apps rather than a Shopify-owned one. It is a small thing, and it is the kind of small thing that tells you how old a comparison article is.

Source: shopify.com/in/dropshipping

### Support

Shopify support comes with the subscription on every plan. Adobe support comes with the licence. Magento Open Source comes with a forum, a Slack channel and whoever you have retained. Free software has never meant free help, and the businesses that get burned here are the ones that budgeted for the licence and not for the person.

Source: www.identixweb.com

### Feature checklists, and why I stopped trusting them

Vendor comparison pages exist to be won by the vendor who published them. Shopify’s own page comparing itself to Magento is a sales asset, and Adobe’s equivalent is too. Use them to find out what a platform thinks is important, not to settle the question.

Source: www.shopify.com

## Switching later is not a feature

Both directions are possible and neither is cheap. Products, customers, orders and URLs can be moved with migration tools. What does not move is the front end, the integrations, the app-specific data and the search rankings attached to your old URL structure. Plan a redirect map before anything else, because that is the part people forget and then spend six months recovering from.

I have written before about rented land. I lost two companies before Pixel Street, and the lesson that survived both failures is simple: never build your main asset on ground someone else controls. A hosted store is a lease. That is a perfectly rational thing to sign when the alternative costs more than it returns, but sign it knowing what it is. Keep your product data, your customer list and your content exportable, and the lease stays a choice rather than a trap.

## So which one

Shopify
Adobe Commerce
Magento Open Source

No in-house developers, and the store must be run by the marketing team
Enterprise catalogue, complex B2B rules, or multi-brand and multi-region operations
You already employ PHP developers and intend to keep employing them

You want a published price you can plan a budget against
Procurement can handle a quoted licence and a build project
Transaction volume high enough that a platform fee hurts more than a salary

Launch date matters more than structural flexibility
You need Adobe’s wider stack, or SaaS operations with an availability commitment
You want to own the code and accept owning the patching

Uptime and PCI compliance should be somebody else’s job
The store is large enough that platform downtime has a rupee value per hour
You are comfortable tracking Adobe’s support windows, or moving to a community distribution

If you are weighing the open-source route more broadly, the closer fight is not this one. It is Shopify against WooCommerce, which is the comparison most Indian small businesses are actually running, and the prices in that post come from the same Shopify pricing page as the table above.

## Questions I get asked

### Is Magento free?

Magento Open Source is free to download and run. Adobe Commerce is not, and Adobe does not publish its price. Free also excludes hosting, the build, extensions and the person who applies security patches, which is why “free” and “cheap” are different words.

### Is Magento dead?

No. Version 2.4.9 shipped in May 2026 and the community distribution Mage-OS shipped 3.2.0 in July 2026. What is true is that it is a much smaller slice of the web than Shopify, that Adobe’s attention is on the paid product, and that extended security patches are reserved for Adobe Commerce customers.

### What does Adobe Commerce cost?

Whatever Adobe quotes you. The ladders you find online, the $22,000 figure among them, come from agencies illustrating a budget conversation, and at least one of them says so in its own small print. Ask for the quote, then price the hosting, build and upgrade retainer separately.

### Can I run a Shopify store from India without Shopify Payments?

Yes, and you have no other option, because India is not on the list of countries where Shopify Payments is offered. Budget for the platform fee on your plan on top of your gateway’s charges, and choose your plan by working out where the fee saving overtakes the higher subscription.

### We are on an old Magento version. Should we move to Shopify or upgrade?

Check your version against Adobe’s support dates first. If you are on 2.4.6 you are out of regular support in August 2026. After that the choice is an upgrade project, a move to a community distribution, or a replatform, and the deciding factor is usually whether you have a developer to hand, not which platform is better. Budgeting help is in our breakdown of what web design actually costs in Kolkata.

## What I would tell you across a table

Pick the platform that matches the team you actually have, not the team you plan to hire. Then spend the argument you saved on the things that move revenue: photography, product copy that says something specific, a checkout you have watched real customers use.

Our eCommerce team at Pixel Street works with both platforms, and the first thing we do on a platform call is ask who will run the store day to day. If you want that conversation, or a second opinion on a quote you have already been given, our eCommerce development services page has the details.

# A Comprehensive Guide to Branding Process

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/complete-branding-process/
Published: July 6, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: Branding

Every prospective client asks what our process is, and almost nobody asks the question they actually mean, which is: at what point do I lose the ability to change my mind cheaply? That is the only thing a branding process is really for. It is a schedule of decisions, arranged so the expensive ones happen after the cheap ones, and so nobody is redesigning a logo in week nine because the positioning was never settled in week two.

I run Pixel Street, a design and branding studio in Salt Lake, Kolkata. We work with brands including Coca-Cola, ITC and Marico, and before Pixel Street I lost two companies of my own. So this is written from the studio side of the table by someone who has also been the client paying for a rework. I have tried to describe what happens at each stage and what tends to go wrong there, rather than what each stage is called.

## The short version

Branding runs in two halves. The first is strategic and produces a document: who you are for, what you stand against, what you will not do. The second is expressive and produces assets: identity, messaging, guidelines, the things people actually see. Doing the second before the first is the single most common and most expensive mistake in this business, and it is expensive because visual work is where the money goes.

This page is the engagement in order. The strategy document itself, and how to write one that rules things out, is the guide to building a brand strategy. Whether you should be trying to break your category at all is the case for and against a disruptive brand. If what you are really doing is changing an existing brand rather than starting one, go to the rebranding roadmap instead, because the sequence is different and the risks are larger.

Stage
What gets decided
How it usually fails

1. StrategyAudience, position, what you refuseWritten so agreeably it rules nothing out
2. IdentityLogo, colour, type, imageryStarted before stage one is signed
3. MessagingName lines, proof, toneTagline written by committee
4. AssetsSite, packaging, collateralScope discovered late, one item at a time
5. GuidelinesRules for reuseDelivered as a PDF nobody opens
6. CommunicationChannels and cadenceChannel chosen first, position retrofitted
7. ReviewWhat changed in perceptionMeasured against nothing recorded at the start
8. AdvocacyHow customers repeat youTreated as a campaign, not an outcome

## Understanding Branding

A brand is what people say about you when you are not in the room. That definition is old and slightly worn, and it survives because it puts the brand outside the company, where it belongs. You do not own it. You own the inputs.

Which is why I am wary of the benefit lists this kind of page usually carries: builds trust, commands premium pricing, increases recall, drives loyalty. Each of those is a claim about what customers will do, made in a document written by the company. They are outcomes you might earn, not features you have bought. Branding work makes them possible; it does not deliver them, and no studio that tells you otherwise can show you the arithmetic.

What the work does reliably do is narrower and worth paying for. It makes you legible. A person who encounters you three times in three places should be able to tell it was the same company, understand roughly what you sell, and form some opinion about whether it is for them. Most small companies fail that test, not because their design is poor but because every touchpoint was made by a different person on a different day with no rule to follow.

### The four things being built

- Brand identity: the name, mark, colour, type and imagery. The part everyone means when they say branding, and a smaller share of the job than they expect.

- Brand personality: the human traits attached to the company, which decide how the identity is used rather than what it looks like.

- Brand messaging: the sentences. What you say first, what you say when challenged, what you never claim.

- Brand experience: everything the customer actually touches, which is where most brands quietly contradict their own guidelines.

## Branding Process

Eight stages, in the order they have to happen. The order matters more than the stage names; every one of them depends on a decision made in the one before it, which is why skipping ahead feels fast and costs more.

### Step 1: Define Your Brand Strategy

Purpose, audience, position, and the things you are ruling out. This stage produces a document, not a design, and its quality is measured by what it forbids. A strategy that a competitor could adopt unchanged has decided nothing.

The stage goes wrong when it is run as a workshop that everyone enjoys. Agreeable sessions produce agreeable documents. The useful version of this meeting has an argument in it, usually about a customer segment somebody in the room does not want to give up. That argument is the deliverable. The brand strategy guide sets out the questions worth having it over.

### Step 2: Craft Your Brand Identity

Now the strategy becomes something you can see. Identity is the mark, the shapes around it, the palette, the typefaces and the imagery, and they are chosen together because they only work together.

#### Brand logo:

The mark carries recognition and nothing else. It does not explain what you sell and it should not try. The tests I actually apply are the boring ones: does it survive black and white, does it survive sixteen pixels, does it survive being cropped to a circle by a social platform that did not ask you. This is one stage inside the wider engagement and it has its own sequence, which is in the logo design process.

#### Shape:

Shape work extends past the mark into backgrounds, layouts, packaging and cards. It is the cheapest element to be consistent about and the one most often left undecided, which is why so many small brands have a considered logo sitting on top of arbitrary boxes.

#### Colour scheme and palette:

Pick a palette, write it down as values, and use it everywhere. That is the whole requirement, and it is harder than it sounds because the palette has to survive a printer, a phone at low brightness and somebody in accounts using the wrong blue in a spreadsheet.

What I will not do here is tell you what colours mean. Colour psychology in marketing is the least reliable material in the whole field: the recognisable figures, including the claim that colour lifts brand recognition by up to eighty per cent, trace back through a chain of citations to a colour consultancy's own web page and stop there, and the researcher usually named alongside the number published on how people read pie charts. Choose colours that distinguish you from the specific competitors a customer sees you next to. That is a real constraint. The rest is decoration dressed as science.

#### Brand voice:

Voice is a constraint, not a style. Write it as pairs, because a single adjective gives a copywriter nothing to push against: warm but not chatty, expert but not lecturing, confident but not loud. Then apply it to something hard, like a refund refusal or a price rise. Voice guidelines that only cover the good news are untested.

#### Positioning and style:

Positioning is decided in stage one; what happens here is translating it into a style somebody else can follow. Language choices, tone, how products are described, what a photograph is allowed to look like. If two people write a product description independently and the results do not sound related, the style guide is not finished.

#### Typography and imagery:

Choose type for reading first and character second. A face that is distinctive at poster size and unreadable in a nine-point form has failed, because the form is where your customers spend their time. Check it at the smallest size you will ever set it, on the worst screen you can find, before you fall in love with the specimen. There is more on this in the principles of typography.

Imagery is the element clients underestimate. Gradients, patterns, packaging and photography carry more of the recognition load than the logo does, because there is more of them on any given page.

#### Interactions:

Every company has a service voice whether it has written one or not. Support email, phone manner, the tone of a complaint reply, the message on a delayed order. These are usually written by whoever is on shift, and they are where the brand is contradicted most often, because nobody sends the guidelines to the person answering at nine at night.

#### UX and UI:

The site is where the identity meets the actual constraint of use. Interface work has its own rules, and they beat brand preferences every time they conflict: a colour that fails contrast is not a brand asset, it is an inaccessible one. Where a guideline and usability disagree, change the guideline.

#### Sound:

Sound matters if you advertise in video or audio, and not much otherwise. Decide it when you need it. Most small brands are told to build a sonic identity years before they have anywhere to play it.

### Step 3: Create Brand Messaging

Messaging is what you say, in what order, and what you refuse to claim. The first line a stranger reads about you is worth more work than the logo and gets a fraction of it.

Tagline or slogan

A tagline is optional. I say that at the start of this conversation because clients often arrive believing it is compulsory, and a bad one is worse than none: it takes up the most valuable line on the page to say something no competitor would dispute.

Three famous taglines get listed as evidence for this, and the list is a better argument than the one it is usually making. Nike launched Just Do It in 1988, and when Nike ran a campaign around it in September 2025 the company's own announcement called that a reintroduction, not a replacement. Coca-Cola's Taste the Feeling arrived in 2016 and was retired in September 2021, when Real Magic was announced as the first new global platform for the trademark since 2016. Subway's Eat Fresh was absorbed into a menu campaign called the Eat Fresh Refresh in July 2021 and has been reworked regionally since.

So of the three lines this page once called timeless, one has survived thirty-seven years and two were changed within a decade — and I only found that out by checking, which nobody does. That is the useful test. A line that is genuinely working gets kept by its owner for decades against considerable internal pressure to do something new. Most lines are not working, which is why most of them get replaced quietly.

### Step 4: Build Brand Assets

Business cards, packaging, decks, signage, the website. This is the stage where budgets are actually spent, and where scope arrives late and one item at a time.

The way to control it is to list every asset before design starts, including the ones nobody thinks of: the invoice, the email signature, the sticker on the carton, the banner for a trade stand in a hall with bad lighting. An asset discovered after the guidelines are signed gets designed by whoever is free, and that is how a brand starts drifting in month two.

### Step 5: Establish Brand Guidelines

Guidelines exist so that people who were not in any of these meetings can make something correct without asking. Judge them by that test alone.

Most brand guidelines fail it, because they are written as a document about the brand rather than as instructions for a stranger. A junior marketer needs the colour values in a form they can paste, the logo in the file types they will be asked for, the two type sizes that cover most cases, and a page of things not to do with worked examples. A long manifesto about brand essence is a portfolio piece for the agency that made it.

### Step 6: Implement Brand Communication

Now the identity meets the market. Channels, cadence, who publishes, who approves. The rule from stage one applies here and gets ignored here: the channel is chosen because the position points at it, not the other way round.

The practical failure at this stage is the approval chain. If four people can veto a post and nobody can commission one, output collapses to whatever is uncontroversial, which is exactly what a distinctive position was supposed to avoid. Name the person who can say yes before the first post goes out.

### Step 7: Monitor and Evolve Your Brand

You cannot measure a change in perception without a record of what perception was before. Take the measurement in stage one, when it is boring to do and nobody wants to: what customers currently say you are, what they think you cost, which competitor they name next to you.

Then be patient with the clock. Positioning shows up in what people say about you unprompted, and that lags by quarters, not weeks. Anyone offering a thirty-day proof point is measuring a campaign.

Distinguish maintenance from change. Adjusting how a position is expressed is normal and should happen continuously. Changing the position is a rebrand, with the costs and risks set out in the rebranding roadmap.

### Step 8: Foster Brand Advocacy

Advocacy is an outcome, not a stage you can run. What you can do is make yourself easy to repeat. If a customer cannot describe you in one sentence to a friend, they will not, however satisfied they are.

That sentence is the real test of everything above. Write down what you want it to be at the start of the project, then ask three actual customers at the end and compare. The gap between the two is the honest scorecard for the whole engagement.

## Common questions about the branding process

### Can I skip straight to the logo?

You can, and people do. What you are buying is a mark chosen against no criteria, which means the review meeting becomes a taste contest and the result gets revisited within a year. If budget is the constraint, do a small strategy stage rather than none.

### Do I need all eight stages?

The order is compulsory; the depth is not. A three-person company needs stages one, two, three and five in a light form, and can defer four and six until there is something to spend them on. What does not work is running them out of sequence.

### What does the client actually have to supply?

Access, mostly. Time with whoever makes decisions, honest answers about competitors and pricing, and a named decision-maker who can approve without a committee. Projects stall on availability far more often than on creative disagreement.

### How do I know the guidelines worked?

Hand them to somebody who was not involved and ask them to produce something simple, like a social post or a one-page flyer. Whatever they get wrong is a defect in the guidelines, not in them.

## Where I would start

If you take one thing from this page, take the order. Strategy, then identity, then messaging, then everything else. The reason it is worth being stubborn about is financial rather than aesthetic: decisions made in stage one cost a meeting to change, and the same decisions made in stage four cost a reprint, a rebuild and an apology to a client who already approved something.

If you want that argued out rather than run as a template, it is the work we do at our branding studio in Kolkata. Bring the competitor you are most worried about and the customer you are least willing to lose, and Pixel Street can start from there. Small companies usually get more out of the strategy stage than large ones, because they have fewer places to hide an unclear position.

# Personal Branding: What the Evidence Actually Supports

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/personal-branding-guide/
Published: July 6, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: Branding

Four years ago I made a cold call to ITC with a fancy deck and zero credibility. The deck was fine. The problem was that nobody on the other end had a reason to believe the person holding it, and no amount of design fixes that. Today we design for ITC, and for Coca-Cola and Marico. The lesson I keep coming back to from that call is that credibility compounds: the first mention is the hardest, and every one after it is easier, because there is finally something to check you against.

I run Pixel Street, a design and branding studio in Salt Lake, Kolkata, and I lost two companies before this one. So the argument I want to make is an unfashionable one. For most professionals, a personal brand is not an audience. It is a reputation held by a few dozen people who are in a position to send you work, and the tactics that grow the first are often the ones that quietly damage the second.

## The short version

Your personal brand already exists. It is whatever the people who have worked with you say about you when you are not in the room, and it was built by your work and your behaviour long before you opened a content calendar. Personal branding is the deliberate management of that, not the manufacture of it.

Which means the useful question is not how to build a personal brand. It is which of the two jobs you are actually doing: deepening trust with a known, small audience, or building reach with an unknown, large one. Almost everyone needs the first and spends their effort on the second.

If you are working on the brand of a company rather than a person, the sequence is different and it is written up separately: the brand strategy guide covers the decisions, the branding process covers the order they happen in, and the case for and against a disruptive brand covers whether to break your category at all.

### Who can have a Personal Brand?

Everyone already does, which is the part that gets skipped. Among your colleagues, clients, former bosses and the people who sat next to you in your first job, you have a reputation. You did not opt into it. The only real choice is whether you take any interest in shaping it.

That reframing matters because it changes what counts as work. If a personal brand were something you built from nothing, then posting would be the work. Since it is a reputation you already have, the work is mostly evidence: doing things that are worth saying about you, and then making them findable by the people who might repeat them.

It also lowers the stakes usefully. You do not need to become known to a hundred thousand strangers. You need the twenty people who could refer you to be able to describe what you do in one sentence, without hedging.

### Why is Personal Branding important?

Because people check. A 2017 CareerBuilder survey of 2,380 US hiring and HR managers, run by Harris Poll, found 70% of employers screening candidates on social media before hiring, up from 11% in 2006, and 51% researching current employees the same way. I am citing that with its date attached on purpose: CareerBuilder has not published a comparable edition since, so it is evidence that the behaviour became normal, not a reading of where the number sits today. Anyone quoting it as a current figure is quoting a nine-year-old survey without saying so.

The wider point survives the staleness. Before a serious conversation, someone will look you up, and whatever they find is doing the arguing on your behalf while you are not there.

There is a line about this that is attributed to Jeff Bezos everywhere, usually as "your brand is what people say about you when you are not in the room." I have not been able to find a primary source for it. Not an interview, not a shareholder letter, not a book. It circulates on quote sites and agency blogs, each citing the last. I still think it is the truest sentence about the subject, which is why it appears here without a name attached rather than with one I cannot stand up.

## Express Benefits of Having a Personal Brand

Four things genuinely change when your reputation is legible to the people around you, and one thing that gets promised does not.

Shorter proof cycles. The gap between meeting someone and being trusted enough to be paid is where most independent careers are won or lost. A legible reputation shortens it, because part of the case has already been made by someone else.

Better-qualified enquiries. A clear public position filters as much as it attracts. When people arrive already knowing what you do and roughly what you charge, you spend less of your life writing proposals for work you were never going to get.

Leverage in the room. Reputation is what lets you say no to a bad brief without losing the client. Nobody negotiates well from a position where every project is the one keeping the lights on, and the work shows it.

Collaboration instead of competition. This is the real structural difference from company branding. In my line of work the other studios are not the enemy, because overflow and referral travel between people who know what each other is good at. That only happens if your peers can describe what you do.

What it does not do is sell for you. A strong personal brand gets you a fair hearing. It does not survive a bad product, a missed deadline or a rude email, and it degrades faster than it accumulates.

## How do you create your Personal Brand?

You cannot create it, because it already exists in some form as a result of every working relationship you have had. What you can do is decide what you want it to say, then close the distance between that and what it currently says.

Here is the order I would work in.

### Step1.: Determine your goals

Write down what you want the reputation to produce. Not adjectives. Outcomes: a specific kind of client, a job at a specific kind of company, speaking invitations, a book, hiring leverage. The reason to be this literal is that the tactics diverge almost immediately. Building toward inbound consulting work looks nothing like building toward a salaried role, and the person doing both at once usually achieves neither.

Then write down the honest version of where you are now. Ask three people who have worked with you to describe what you do, in their words, and do not defend yourself while they answer. The distance between their sentence and your intended sentence is the entire project. Everything below is closing it.

### Step2.: Uncover your audience

Name the people whose opinion of you would change your year. In most cases the list is short enough to write on one page, and it is rarely the same as the list of people who like your posts.

Do that exercise properly and it will contradict your instincts about channels. If the twelve people who matter are procurement heads at consumer goods companies in India, then a large following of designers is pleasant and irrelevant. If they are founders, it may be the opposite. The audience decides the channel; the channel does not decide the audience.

### Step3.: Analyze your peers

This is where personal branding genuinely differs from company branding. A brand strategy has to name an opponent, because positioning is comparative. A personal reputation does not work that way. The peers in your field are the primary route through which your name travels, and treating them as competitors cuts the wire it travels along.

So study them, but study them for gaps rather than for weaknesses. What does nobody in your city write about honestly? What question do clients keep asking that the whole industry answers with a brochure? That gap is where a small, specific reputation is available, and it is usually available because saying the true thing costs something.

### Step4.: Define your difference

Specificity is the whole game, and it is almost always achieved by subtraction. "Designer" is a category. "I run a studio in Kolkata that does brand and web work for large consumer companies, and I have lost two companies of my own" describes exactly one person. The second sentence is not more impressive than the first. It is more useful, because it can be repeated accurately by someone else.

Test yours by handing it to a friend and asking them to introduce you with it. If they have to add a clause to make it make sense, it is not finished. If they can say it in one breath and it excludes some work you would have taken, it is.

### Step5.: Work toward being your most authentic self

Authenticity has been flattened into a content style, which is a shame, because the operational meaning is simple and hard: say only things you would still say to the person's face, and publish opinions you are willing to be argued with about.

The practical benefit is consistency. A position you actually hold survives being asked about at a meeting eighteen months later. A position adopted because it performed well does not, and the failure is public and expensive. My own test before publishing anything is whether I would defend it to a client who disagrees. If the answer is no, the piece is not honest, it is marketing wearing honesty as a costume.

### Step6.: Give value

The most reliable form of value is specific and unscalable: answering the actual question someone asked, introducing two people who should know each other, telling a founder their brief is wrong before they pay you to execute it. None of that is content. All of it is what people repeat about you later.

Published work matters too, but the bar is that it should cost you something to publish. A post that reveals how you price, what you got wrong, or which fashionable tactic you have stopped believing in is worth twenty that summarise what everyone already agrees on.

### Step7.: Collaborate with your peers

Reputation travels through people, not through platforms. The mechanism is someone saying your name in a room you are not in, and that only happens if they can remember what you are for and have some reason to want you to do well.

Collaboration is the cheapest way to earn both. Working alongside someone for a month tells them more about you than three years of following you would, and it puts you in front of their network with an implicit endorsement attached. If you are thinking about this at scale, the mechanics of borrowed audience are covered in how local influencers can grow a brand beyond their own city.

## Nurture and harness your personality

Some things worth keeping in view while you do the work above.

In personal branding you are the medium, and your temperament decides which tactics are available to you. If you are energised by people, run on conversation: events, calls, podcasts, the phone. If you are not, write. Introverts are routinely told to network their way into a reputation and then fail at it slowly for years, when a body of written work would have done the same job better and been searchable afterwards.

Know your weaknesses precisely enough to design around them rather than apologise for them. Mine is that I would rather argue with a client about their positioning than post about it, which is a real cost, and writing things down like this is the workaround rather than the preference.

### Get creative and consistent with your content:

Consistency is worth more than volume, and it means consistency of position, not of posting schedule. Somebody who publishes four times a year and says the same defensible thing each time is more legible than somebody who publishes weekly and drifts with whatever is being discussed.

Match the format to how you actually think. If writing is slow for you, talk: record it, transcribe it, edit the transcript. The medium is negotiable. The requirement that you have a point of view is not.

### Don't be afraid to show your vulnerability:

There is a version of this that is a performance, and it is worse than saying nothing. The useful version is specific: a decision you got wrong, what it cost, and what you do differently now. I lost two companies before Pixel Street and I say so in most things I write, including this one, because the alternative is presenting a career as a straight line that nobody would recognise.

The distinction is whether the story has a fact in it. Confessional writing with no verifiable detail reads as technique, because it is.

### Choose the right social media platform:

Pick where your named audience already is and ignore the rest, including the platform everyone is currently excited about. For most professional services in India that means LinkedIn, plus wherever your specific industry actually talks. X has a far smaller professional audience than its share of discourse suggests. Instagram works if your output is visual and does very little if it is not.

One platform done properly beats four done thinly, and a page you own beats all of them for anything you want to survive an algorithm change. The argument against building your main asset on ground someone else controls applies to a reputation exactly as it applies to a company website.

### Provide value at every opportunity and never share without a purpose:

Before publishing, be able to answer what this is for and who it is for. Not commercially, necessarily, but honestly. Sharing to stay visible produces the volume of noise that makes people scroll past your name, which is the opposite of the goal.

## Prominent examples of Personal Brands

Every article on this subject names the same four people. I have kept them, because they are instructive, but not in the way these lists usually intend. Each one is a poor template for a normal professional career, and understanding why is more useful than admiring them.

### Oprah Winfrey:

The clearest case of a personal brand built on a body of work rather than on commentary about work. Twenty-five years of a daily show is the asset; everything downstream of it, including the media company and the book club's ability to move a title, is interest earned on that. The lesson usually drawn is about authenticity. The lesson actually available is that she made an enormous quantity of the thing itself first.

### Elon Musk:

The most-followed account on X, and the reason to study him is that his reputation is now inseparable from his companies in both directions. The upside and the damage both transfer. That is the real trade in fusing a person to a business, and most people recommending it have never carried the downside. Ignore the follower counts these write-ups quote, including for him; they are stale within months and were never the thing worth studying.

### Richard Branson:

Virgin is the interesting case because the reputation became a licensable asset. The group mixes businesses it owns with names it licenses to other operators, which is why published counts of "how many Virgin companies there are" vary so wildly and why I have not repeated one. What Branson demonstrates is that a personal brand can be strong enough to rent out. That is rare, and it is a different thing from being well known.

### Gary Vaynerchuk:

Chairman of VaynerX and chief executive of VaynerMedia, both operating. He is the most copied and least copyable of the four. The volume strategy works when the volume is the product, and he has built an agency group underneath it that converts attention into revenue. Without that machine, the same posting schedule produces exhaustion and a following that cannot be sold anything.

## Two numbers in this field that do not survive checking

You will meet a figure of 43% for employers using social media to check on current employees, usually alongside the 70% above. It appears nowhere in the CareerBuilder research it is attributed to. That release puts research into current employees at 51%.

The other is that 84% of Millennials trust neither advertisements nor the brands that create them, which is a misreading of the source it travels with. The McCarthy Group's 2014 survey question was whether respondents were the kind of person who likes advertising. Liking is not trusting, the question said nothing about brands, and the published page discloses no sample size. The argument it usually props up, that people trust people rather than logos, stands perfectly well without it.

## Questions I get asked about this

### Do I need a personal brand if I am not a founder?

You have one either way. Whether to invest in it depends on how much of your future work arrives through people who already know you. For most consultants, freelancers, agency owners and senior specialists, that is nearly all of it.

### How long before it produces anything?

Longer than a campaign and shorter than people fear. The first effect is usually qualitative: enquiries arrive already knowing what you do, so conversations start further along. Anyone promising a measurable pipeline in thirty days is describing advertising.

### Is a personal brand a risk if I want to sell my company later?

It is a real one, and it is the honest argument against everything above. A business whose enquiries all arrive through one person's name is harder to sell than one whose enquiries arrive through a company's. If an exit is the plan, build the studio's reputation deliberately alongside your own.

### What is the single highest-return thing to do first?

Write one page explaining what you actually believe about your field, including the part your industry would dispute, and put it somewhere you own. It does more than a year of sharing other people's articles.

## Conclusion

Personal branding has been oversold as a route to becoming famous and undersold as what it actually is: taking responsibility for a reputation you already have. The work is unglamorous. Do good work, be specific about what you do, say things you are willing to defend, and make it easy for the people who already rate you to explain you to somebody else.

None of that looks like a personal branding strategy while it is happening. It looks like work, and like being the same person in public that you are in a meeting. The compounding comes later, and only if there was something underneath it worth compounding.

If you would rather argue about your positioning with someone than fill in a template, that is the work we do at Pixel Street in Kolkata.

# No-Code Web Development: What Survived Since 2023

URL: https://pixelstreet.in/blog/no-code-web-development-guide/
Published: July 5, 2023
Author: Khurshid Alam
Categories: WEB DEVELOPMENT

I published this guide in 2023 and told you to look at Editor X, Integromat and Makerpad. All three are gone.

That is not a sentence I enjoy writing. It is also the most useful thing this page can tell you about no-code web development, so it goes at the top rather than in a quiet update note at the bottom.

I run Pixel Street, a web design studio in Salt Lake, Kolkata. We design and build for brands like Coca-Cola, ITC and Marico. No-code platforms are supposed to be the thing that makes a studio like mine unnecessary, and for a narrow band of work they genuinely are. So this is the honest version. What these tools cost right now, what their free tiers actually allow after several years of quiet tightening, which ones died, and the specific point where a no-code build stops being the cheap option.

Every price below was read off the vendor's own pricing page on 30 July 2026. They will move. That is rather the point.

## The short answer

No-code is excellent for internal tools, prototypes, single-purpose landing pages and small brochure sites. It is a poor bet for anything that has to be a durable, differentiated revenue channel. The reason is not that the software is bad. It is that you are renting a platform whose prices, plan names and free tiers change under you, and whose export options range from partial to nonexistent. Since the first version of this guide, entry prices rose, three of the named tools stopped existing, most free tiers were cut, and the industry moved from flat monthly fees to metered billing where your bill grows with your traffic. Budget for the meter, not the sticker.

## What the 2023 version of this guide got wrong

I am scoring my own homework here because a comparison post that never audits itself is worthless. Here is what happened to the tools this page recommended.

Named in the 2023 guide
Status on 30 July 2026

Editor X, "the Wix alternative for professionals", at $22 to $75/month
Discontinued. Wix's help centre says Editor X completed the transition to Wix Studio in January 2025, existing sites were updated automatically, and it is no longer possible to create new Editor X sites. editorx.com now redirects to the Wix Studio page.

Integromat, recommended as the Zapier alternative
Gone under that name. integromat.com now redirects to a shutdown notice on make.com. The product is Make, and its plan structure was rebuilt around credits.

Makerpad, listed as a leading no-code community
Gone. makerpad.co today serves an unrelated product about building AI companies that run themselves. The no-code learning community that name referred to is not there.

Thirteen dollar prices across Webflow, Wix, Squarespace, Bubble, Editor X and Shopify
Not one is still correct. Several plans no longer exist by name.

Three dead names and thirteen wrong numbers in roughly three years. If you are deciding where to build something you intend to still own in 2029, that mortality rate is the finding. Everything below is written with it in mind.

## What no-code actually costs in July 2026

Two things jump out of that table. The spread between the cheapest serious option and the most expensive is now roughly ten times, for tools that all describe themselves as no-code. And Glide, which most people still think of as a spreadsheet-to-app toy, has a first paid tier of $199 a month.

## The free tiers were quietly hollowed out

This is the change almost nobody writes about, and it is the one that will actually catch you.

The 2023 version of this page said, correctly at the time, that you could get a long way for nothing. That is much less true now. Read the current numbers again in one place:

- Airtable allows 1,000 records per base and 100 automation runs a month on free. A single moderately busy contact form eats that.

- Zapier allows 100 tasks a month, and only two-step Zaps. Any workflow with a filter and two destinations is a paid workflow.

- Webflow gives you two static pages and 1 GB of bandwidth on a webflow.io subdomain. That is a demo, not a site.

- Adalo and Bubble both let you build free and then charge you at the exact moment the thing becomes real, which is publishing.

- Make allows 1,000 credits a month and will not run a scenario more often than every fifteen minutes.

The pattern is consistent and deliberate. Free is now a trial with no clock on it. It is generous enough to make you build, and calibrated to stop working at roughly the point where you have sunk enough hours that leaving feels expensive. Softr and Carrd are the honourable exceptions on that list. Softr's free tier includes a custom domain, and Carrd charges $19 a year rather than $19 a month.

## The meter is the real price

The bigger structural change since 2023 is that no-code stopped selling flat monthly fees and started selling metered usage.

Bubble rebuilt its entire pricing around workload units, a measure of the database operations, workflows and web requests your app performs. Exceed your allowance and you either buy a workload tier or pay overages. Glide charges $5 per additional user and two cents per additional update on top of the subscription. Framer charges $20 a month per additional editor and meters AI features in credits. Webflow sells bandwidth in blocks, at $20 a month for 50 GB on top of your plan. Softr meters AI credits. Zapier meters tasks. Make meters credits.

What that means in practice is that your no-code bill is a function of your traffic. The successful version of your project costs more than the failed one, which is fine when you have priced it in and unpleasant when you have not. Adalo is the loud counterexample, marketing flat pricing with "no usage-based charges" as its differentiator, which tells you exactly how the rest of the category behaves.

So when you compare a no-code subscription against a quote for a custom build, compare three years, not one month, and model the meter at the traffic you are actually hoping for.

## What this costs from India, which is different

Almost every no-code comparison you will read prices these tools in dollars for a buyer in California. That changes the answer here, and it changes it by a lot.

Two of these companies genuinely price for India. Shopify bills Indian merchants in rupees, from Rs 1,499 a month on Basic up to Rs 22,680 on Advanced, with POS Pro at Rs 7,000 per location. Squarespace also bills in rupees, at Rs 1,901 a month for Basic and Rs 4,310 for Advanced. Zapier lets you pick INR at checkout.

Webflow, Airtable, Bubble, Framer, Glide, Softr and Adalo do not. Webflow's page states plainly that all prices are in USD, per site, plus applicable taxes. For a Kolkata business that means the sticker price is a floor, and you add conversion and card charges on top of it, every month, forever, on an expense that never converts into an asset you own.

Run the arithmetic on the middle of the range. Bubble's Growth plan at $119 a month is a serious annual commitment in rupee terms for a small Indian business, and at the end of three years of it you own no code. That is the comparison worth making, and it is the same one I make in more detail in Shopify versus WooCommerce for an Indian store.

## Where no-code genuinely wins

Now the part where I argue against my own invoice, because pretending these tools are toys is how agencies lose trust.

Internal tools. This is where no-code is not just acceptable but clearly correct. An ops dashboard, an inventory tracker, an approvals queue, a client portal. Airtable with Softr on top will beat a custom build on time and cost, and nobody outside your company ever sees it, so brand distinctiveness is irrelevant. If you are paying a developer to build an internal CRUD app in 2026, stop.

Prototypes and validation. Testing whether anyone wants the thing before you build the thing. Bubble's free tier exists precisely for this and is good at it.

Single-purpose pages. One campaign, one event, one link-in-bio. Carrd at $19 a year with a custom domain is an absurdly good deal and I recommend it without qualification for that job.

Small brochure sites. A local business that needs to exist online with hours, services and a contact form. Wix or Squarespace will do this fine. You do not need a studio for it, and I would rather say so than sell you something you do not need.

The common thread is that no-code wins wherever the website is not the product, not the brand, and not the growth channel.

## Where it breaks, and what leaving costs

The failure mode is never the build. It is the exit.

Read the export terms before you fall in love with an editor, because they are worse than most people assume. Squarespace's own help centre is unusually blunt about this. Its export produces an .xml file aimed at WordPress, and style settings, custom CSS, product blocks, video blocks, portfolio pages and store pages do not come with it. The same page states that it is not possible to export content from one Squarespace site and import it into another. Leaving Squarespace is not a migration. It is a rebuild with your blog posts salvaged.

Webflow does offer code export, and then charges you for it. It sits on the Core Workspace plan at $19 a month, on top of your site plan. Exporting your own work is a subscription feature.

On the app builders the question does not really arise. A Bubble, Adalo, Glide or Softr application runs on the vendor's own infrastructure, which is why Bubble can meter your database operations in the first place. There is no folder of code to take with you. If the platform reprices, changes direction, or is acquired and wound down, the way Editor X and Integromat were, your options are to accept the new terms or start again.

That risk is not hypothetical for this category, and I have the receipts three paragraphs into this very page. It is also the argument I make at more length in AI website builders versus custom development, which covers the same ownership question from the AI-builder side.

The honest framing is not "no-code is a trap". It is that you are choosing a lease, and leases are fine as long as you know you are signing one and you know the cost of moving out.

## Will no-code replace developers

Production, yes. Judgement, no. And I say that as someone whose studio sells both.

Assembling pages and wiring up CRUD screens is genuinely commoditised now. If a developer's entire value was turning a design into markup, that value has largely evaporated, and no amount of arguing about semantic HTML will bring it back.

What survives is everything upstream of the pixels. What are you selling, who is the competitor, who is the audience, what must this communicate, and where does the communication happen. No prompt and no drag-and-drop canvas answers those. When every business in your category can generate a competent website in an afternoon, the competent website is worth nothing, and the thinking behind it is worth more than it was. I have written about the same shift in what AI is doing to design work.

The useful version of the developer question is narrower anyway. Not "will no-code replace developers" but "can this specific project survive on a platform I do not control". Usually the answer is yes for a while and no eventually, and the skill is knowing which side of that line you are on.

## Where the community actually is now

The 2023 version of this page sent you to Makerpad, No-Code Founders and the no-code subreddit. One of those three no longer exists, which is a fair summary of how fast this space moves.

- Makerpad is gone. The domain now hosts an unrelated AI product. Do not go looking for the tutorials.

- No Code Founders is still running, as a free weekly newsletter and a tools and deals directory, and says it reaches over 38,000 founders a week. It has repositioned heavily towards AI tooling.

- The r/nocode subreddit is still active, and remains the least sponsored place to find out that a tool has quietly changed its pricing.

Vendor documentation is the other underrated source, and it is where I got most of the numbers in this post. Bubble's manual publishes its full price table and its workload rules openly. That is a good sign about a vendor. Wix's pricing page, by contrast, would not show me a stable figure at all, because prices and currency vary by location. Draw your own conclusion about which company expects you to comparison shop.

## How to choose, in three questions

Answer these honestly and the shortlist writes itself.

- Who sees this? If the answer is your own team, use no-code, and use it today. Airtable and Softr, or Glide if you can justify $199 a month. If the answer is your market, keep reading.

- Is this a test or a channel? A test should cost as little and take as short a time as possible, so use the free tier and accept the limits. A channel that has to produce leads and get cited by AI engines is an asset, and assets should be built on ground you control. That is the whole argument in template versus custom web design.

- What does year three cost? Take the entry price, add the metered overages at the traffic you are actually targeting, add the rebuild you will pay for if the tool reprices or disappears, and compare that number against a one-off custom build. Do it in rupees if you are buying from India, because most of these vendors will bill you in dollars.

If you want the CMS side of this decision rather than the builder side, I compared the main options in the guide to CMS platforms.

## FAQ

### Is no-code web development still worth it in 2026?

For internal tools, prototypes and small brochure sites, yes, and more so than in 2023 because the tools got better. For a website that has to differentiate a brand and generate revenue over years, the maths has got worse, not better. Entry prices rose, free tiers shrank, and billing moved to metered usage that scales with your success.

### What happened to Editor X?

Wix folded it into Wix Studio. Wix's help centre states the transition completed in January 2025, existing Editor X sites were updated automatically, and new Editor X sites can no longer be created. If you followed a 2023 recommendation into Editor X, you are on Wix Studio now whether you chose it or not.

### Is Integromat still available?

No. It is Make. The old integromat.com address redirects to a shutdown notice, and the product was rebuilt around a credit model. The free tier now allows 1,000 credits a month with a fifteen-minute minimum interval between runs.

### Which no-code platform has the most usable free tier?

Softr, on the current numbers. Its free plan includes 10 app users, 5,000 database records, 500 workflow actions and a custom domain, which is more than any other free tier here offers. Webflow, Adalo and Bubble free plans will not let you put a real site or app in front of the public at all.

### Do no-code tools cost more for buyers in India?

Effectively yes, for most of them. Shopify and Squarespace bill in rupees and Zapier offers INR at checkout. Webflow, Airtable, Bubble, Framer, Glide, Softr and Adalo bill in US dollars, so an Indian buyer pays the American price plus conversion and card charges, every month.

### Can I export my site if I leave a no-code platform?

Rarely in full. Squarespace exports an .xml file for WordPress that leaves behind your styles, custom CSS, store pages and portfolio pages, and cannot even be imported into another Squarespace site. Webflow offers code export but only on a paid Core Workspace plan at $19 a month. App builders like Bubble, Adalo and Glide run on the vendor's infrastructure, so there is nothing to export. Check this before you build, not after.

### Will these prices still be right next year?

Some of them will not. Every figure on this page was read from the vendor's own pricing page on 30 July 2026, and the last version of this guide had thirteen prices in it that all went stale within three years. Verify against the vendor before you buy.
